parts.title: Enquiring about a hotel vacancy
parts.context: A man phones a hotel to ask about a part-time job.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a man telephoning a hotel to ask about a job. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: joanna
script.text: Good morning, Linden Court Hotel. Joanna speaking.

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: Oh, good morning. I'm phoning about the vacancy you advertised on your website, the one for a receptionist. It's part-time, isn't it?

script.speaker: joanna
script.text: That's right, and it's still open. I deal with the recruitment, so I can take a few details from you and tell you about the post.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The man is asking about a job as a receptionist, so 'receptionist' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: joanna
script.text: Could I have your name, please?

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: Yes, it's Daniel Brewster.

script.speaker: joanna
script.text: Sorry, how do you spell your surname?

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: It's B-R-E-W-S-T-E-R.

script.speaker: joanna
script.text: Thank you. And what are you doing at the moment, Daniel? Are you working?

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: Yes and no. I'm in my final year at university, studying languages, but I help out in a bookshop on Saturdays and in the holidays, serving customers and sorting the new stock.

script.speaker: joanna
script.text: I see. Have you worked in a hotel before?

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: A little. I spent last summer in a hotel kitchen, mostly washing up, but I enjoyed the atmosphere. I've never worked on a front desk, though.

script.speaker: joanna
script.text: That doesn't matter, we train everybody. Now, the job involves dealing with guests from abroad, so do you speak any other languages?

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: Well, I did French at school, but I wouldn't say I was fluent. I'm much better at Spanish. My mother's from Madrid, so we speak it at home.

script.speaker: joanna
script.text: That could be really useful. We get a lot of visitors from Spain in the summer.

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: Good. Now, the advert said twenty hours a week. Is that still right?

script.speaker: joanna
script.text: That was the original plan, but we've had so much demand for evening work that we've put it up to twenty-five.

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: That's fine by me. And what's the pay?

script.speaker: joanna
script.text: It's eleven pounds an hour to start with, rising to thirteen once you've finished your three-month trial period.

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: That sounds reasonable.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: So when would I start, if I got the job?

script.speaker: joanna
script.text: Now, let me see. It says here the first of May. Oh, no, sorry, that's the date from the old advert. We've moved it back a month, so it'll be the first of June.

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: That suits me, because it's after my final exams. Are there any extras with the job?

script.speaker: joanna
script.text: Well, we don't have staff parking, I'm afraid, and the discount on rooms only applies to family members. But there's a staff restaurant, and everybody on duty gets a hot meal there at no charge, which people really appreciate.

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: That's good to know. Will I have to wear a uniform?

script.speaker: joanna
script.text: Yes. We supply the jacket, two shirts and the trousers, and we wash them for you. The only thing you have to buy yourself is a pair of black shoes.

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: That's no problem. How do I apply?

script.speaker: joanna
script.text: Just email your CV and a covering letter. Address it to the general manager, Mr Sutherland, and put the job title in the subject line.

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: Mr Sutherland. Right. And when do you need it by?

script.speaker: joanna
script.text: We're interviewing the week after next, on the Tuesday, so applications have to be in by this Friday.

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: That doesn't give me long, but I'll write it tonight. Thanks very much for your help.

script.speaker: joanna
script.text: You're welcome, Daniel. Good luck.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A tour of a botanic garden
parts.context: A guide welcomes visitors and explains the layout of a botanic garden.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear a guide giving a walking tour of a botanical garden. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: ruth
script.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Haverley Botanic Garden. I'm Ruth, and I'll be your guide today. First, a little background.

script.speaker: ruth
script.text: The garden was founded in 1851. Many people assume it began as a public park, and it's true that factory workers came here on Sundays, but that wasn't the idea. It was set up by Dr Amos Haverley, who taught at the town infirmary. He wanted his students to learn to recognise the plants that medicines are made from. Rare plants from abroad only arrived later.
script.tts: The garden was founded in eighteen fifty-one. Many people assume it began as a public park, and it's true that factory workers came here on Sundays, but that wasn't the idea. It was set up by Dr Amos Haverley, who taught at the town infirmary. He wanted his students to learn to recognise the plants that medicines are made from. Rare plants from abroad only arrived later.

script.speaker: ruth
script.text: Our pride and joy is the Great Glasshouse. By the 1990s it was in a dreadful state and nearly had to be pulled down. We applied to the national heritage fund for a grant, but we were turned down. A local brewery paid for the new roof, which was generous, but it was only a small part of the work. Most of the money came from ordinary people: visitors who dropped coins into collecting boxes, and schools that organised sponsored walks.
script.tts: Our pride and joy is the Great Glasshouse. By the nineteen nineties it was in a dreadful state and nearly had to be pulled down. We applied to the national heritage fund for a grant, but we were turned down. A local brewery paid for the new roof, which was generous, but it was only a small part of the work. Most of the money came from ordinary people: visitors who dropped coins into collecting boxes, and schools that organised sponsored walks.

script.speaker: ruth
script.text: You might imagine our scientists spend their time travelling to remote forests to find new species. They did once, but not any more, and we don't breed new varieties for the garden trade either. Our main work is far less glamorous. In the basement of the visitor centre is a seed bank, where we store seeds of wild plants that are in danger of disappearing for ever.

script.speaker: ruth
script.text: That brings me to our appeal. The heating in the glasshouse is very old, but the council has agreed to pay for a new system. Some volunteers would love a new area of woodland, but there's no funding for that yet. What this year's appeal will pay for is a classroom, where school groups can do experiments. At the moment we teach children in a corridor.

script.speaker: ruth
script.text: A word about when to visit. People say summer is best because of the roses, and they are lovely in June. Early spring is popular too, when the magnolias flower, but one hard frost and the petals turn brown. My own favourite is October, when the maples around the lake turn bright red.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: ruth
script.text: Now, let me explain the layout. Please look at the map. We're at the main entrance, at the bottom, and north is at the top. The visitor centre is just inside the gate on the right. On the left is the café, and between the café and the main path is our plant sales area, which I'd leave until the end. The wide path ahead is the Central Walk, which runs straight up to the glasshouse. We'll start by turning left at the first crossing.

script.speaker: ruth
script.text: Once we've turned left, the café is on your left, and the first bed on your right is the rose garden. It has over two hundred varieties.

script.speaker: ruth
script.text: Now, if you have one of our older leaflets, it shows the herb garden beside the glasshouse. Please ignore that. It was moved last year, because the old site was too shady. It's now a little further along this path, still on the right, directly across from the café.

script.speaker: ruth
script.text: Then we'll go back to the Central Walk and head north. As you walk up, you'll see the sensory garden on your right, with the lake beyond it.

script.speaker: ruth
script.text: When we reach the glasshouse, we'll turn right along the northern path. Once you're past the glasshouse, the bamboo grove is on your left. You'll hear it rustling before you see it.

script.speaker: ruth
script.text: Then we'll double back and carry on west. Just beyond the glasshouse, on the right, is the rock garden. It's a new feature, built where the herb garden used to be.

script.speaker: ruth
script.text: To finish, we'll walk back down to the first crossing and turn east. Keep the lake on your left, and beyond the visitor centre you'll find the orchard on your right, directly across the path from the lake. Right, if there are no questions, shall we make a start? Please follow me.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A survey of regional dialects
parts.context: Two linguistics students discuss a dialect survey with their tutor.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two linguistics students, Tara and Marcus, talking to their tutor, Dr Whitfield, about a survey of regional dialect words. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: whitfield
script.text: Come in, both of you. I've read your draft, and before the results, I'd like to hear how the fieldwork went. Tara, you did most of the interviews, didn't you?

script.speaker: tara
script.text: Mostly, yes. We stood outside the market in Hexley on Saturdays. Some people were in a hurry, of course, but the real difficulty was that they'd say, 'Oh, I haven't got an accent, you want my grandad,' and walk off. They couldn't see why their speech would be of any interest. Once they did stop, nobody minded telling us their age.

script.speaker: whitfield
script.text: That's very common. People assume dialect belongs to somebody else. Now, you used photographs rather than a list of written questions. Why was that?

script.speaker: marcus
script.text: Well, our first idea was to ask, 'What do you call a bread roll?', but then people just repeat your words back to you. With a photograph, they say the first word that comes into their head. It was a bit quicker as well, but that wasn't the reason.

script.speaker: whitfield
script.text: Fine. And did the pilot lead to any changes?

script.speaker: tara
script.text: It took about twenty-five minutes, which was long, but we kept all forty pictures and let people stop whenever they liked. A couple were confusing, like the one meant to be a sofa, which looked more like a bench, but you told us to leave it in, because the confusion was interesting. The one thing we did change was adding a question about where people grew up, not just where they live now.

script.speaker: whitfield
script.text: Good. Now, I do have one worry about your method.

script.speaker: marcus
script.text: It's the prompting, isn't it? When people couldn't think of a word, I sometimes helped them out. 'Is it a cob or a bap?', that sort of thing. Tara said I shouldn't.

script.speaker: whitfield
script.text: She was right. As soon as you suggest a word, you can't be sure it's really theirs. That worries me more than the sample size, or how you wrote the answers down.

script.speaker: marcus
script.text: So should we do those interviews again?

script.speaker: whitfield
script.text: No, you wouldn't have time, and don't throw the data away, either. Mark which answers were prompted, and say so openly in your methods section.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: whitfield
script.text: Right, now the results. You looked at five social factors. Let's take them one at a time. Which came out as the most important?

script.speaker: tara
script.text: Age, by a long way. The over-sixties gave the most local words, for the bread roll, the gym shoes and the narrow passage between houses. The under-thirties mostly gave the standard words you'd hear anywhere in the country.

script.speaker: whitfield
script.text: No surprise there. What about gender?

script.speaker: marcus
script.text: We predicted that women would use fewer local words, because there's a theory that women lean towards the standard form. But our figures show the opposite. Women gave slightly more.

script.speaker: whitfield
script.text: Interesting, but don't claim too much from a small difference. And how long people had lived in the area?

script.speaker: tara
script.text: We wanted to compare long-term residents with newcomers, but only four of our participants had moved to the area in the last ten years, so we can't really say anything.

script.speaker: whitfield
script.text: No, four is far too few. Say so in the report. What about education?

script.speaker: marcus
script.text: We compared people with degrees and people who left school at sixteen, and the answers were very much the same. There's no clear pattern at all.

script.speaker: whitfield
script.text: And the last one, occupation? I noticed the farmers stood out in your table.

script.speaker: tara
script.text: At first sight, yes. They used more local words than any other group. But then we realised nearly all of them were over sixty, so when we took age into account, the difference disappeared.

script.speaker: whitfield
script.text: Good. That's exactly the kind of check I wanted to see.

script.speaker: marcus
script.text: Thank you, Dr Whitfield.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: the history of the bicycle
parts.context: A lecture about how the bicycle developed in the nineteenth century.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about the history of the bicycle. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good afternoon. Today I want to trace the history of the bicycle. It's a machine so familiar that we tend to assume it was invented in a single moment by a single genius. In reality, the design we know took nearly seventy years to arrive, and almost every step began as an attempt to fix a problem with the one before.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The story begins in Germany in 1817, with Karl von Drais. He's often described as a baron, and he certainly was an inventor, but his actual job was as a forester, managing woodland in the state of Baden. His machine had two wheels in a line, a wooden frame and a handle for steering, but no pedals. The rider simply pushed along the ground with their feet. Historians think he was prompted by a crisis. In 1816, after a huge volcanic eruption on the other side of the world, Europe had no real summer. Harvests failed, and the price of oats rose so high that many horses had to be killed. Suddenly there was a demand for a way of getting about without one.
script.tts: The story begins in Germany in eighteen seventeen, with Karl von Drais. He's often described as a baron, and he certainly was an inventor, but his actual job was as a forester, managing woodland in the state of Baden. His machine had two wheels in a line, a wooden frame and a handle for steering, but no pedals. The rider simply pushed along the ground with their feet. Historians think he was prompted by a crisis. In eighteen sixteen, after a huge volcanic eruption on the other side of the world, Europe had no real summer. Harvests failed, and the price of oats rose so high that many horses had to be killed. Suddenly there was a demand for a way of getting about without one.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The machine became a craze in England, where it was taken up by fashionable young men, and so it was nicknamed the dandy horse. Some people called it the hobby horse, but the name that stuck was dandy. The craze didn't last, partly because riders kept colliding with pedestrians, and several cities banned them from the pavement.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The next breakthrough came in France in the 1860s, when makers fixed pedals directly to the front wheel. For the first time, a rider could move without touching the ground. These machines were heavy, with wooden wheels and iron rims, and anyone who rode one over cobbles soon understood why it was nicknamed the boneshaker.
script.tts: The next breakthrough came in France in the eighteen sixties, when makers fixed pedals directly to the front wheel. For the first time, a rider could move without touching the ground. These machines were heavy, with wooden wheels and iron rims, and anyone who rode one over cobbles soon understood why it was nicknamed the boneshaker.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Then, in the 1870s, came the high-wheeler, later nicknamed the penny-farthing after two British coins of very different sizes. Because the pedals were attached to the front wheel, one turn of the pedals meant exactly one turn of the wheel. So the bigger the wheel, the greater the distance you covered each time, and some wheels were taller than a man's waist. This was fast but frightening. If the wheel hit a stone, the rider was thrown forward over the handlebars, which was known as taking a header.
script.tts: Then, in the eighteen seventies, came the high-wheeler, later nicknamed the penny-farthing after two British coins of very different sizes. Because the pedals were attached to the front wheel, one turn of the pedals meant exactly one turn of the wheel. So the bigger the wheel, the greater the distance you covered each time, and some wheels were taller than a man's waist. This was fast but frightening. If the wheel hit a stone, the rider was thrown forward over the handlebars, which was known as taking a header.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The solution came in 1885, from an English manufacturer, John Kemp Starley. His Rover was the first really successful safety bicycle. Its wheels were almost the same size, so the rider sat low down, and instead of attaching the pedals to the wheel, Starley used a chain to drive the back one. That meant the wheel size no longer mattered, and gears could be added later. Nearly every bicycle since has followed this plan.
script.tts: The solution came in eighteen eighty-five, from an English manufacturer, John Kemp Starley. His Rover was the first really successful safety bicycle. Its wheels were almost the same size, so the rider sat low down, and instead of attaching the pedals to the wheel, Starley used a chain to drive the back one. That meant the wheel size no longer mattered, and gears could be added later. Nearly every bicycle since has followed this plan.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: One thing still spoiled the ride, though: solid rubber tyres. In 1888, a Scottish vet, John Dunlop, tried to make his young son's tricycle more comfortable. He wrapped a rubber tube around each wheel and filled it with air. This pneumatic tyre made riding smoother, and it made bicycles faster as well.
script.tts: One thing still spoiled the ride, though: solid rubber tyres. In eighteen eighty-eight, a Scottish vet, John Dunlop, tried to make his young son's tricycle more comfortable. He wrapped a rubber tube around each wheel and filled it with air. This pneumatic tyre made riding smoother, and it made bicycles faster as well.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: By the 1890s, a cycling craze had swept Europe and North America, and its social effects were enormous, especially for women. A young woman on a bicycle could visit friends, travel to work or just go out for the day without a chaperone, and the independence this gave alarmed many of their parents. Women also demanded more practical clothing, and long skirts gave way to shorter ones, and even to trousers called bloomers.
script.tts: By the eighteen nineties, a cycling craze had swept Europe and North America, and its social effects were enormous, especially for women. A young woman on a bicycle could visit friends, travel to work or just go out for the day without a chaperone, and the independence this gave alarmed many of their parents. Women also demanded more practical clothing, and long skirts gave way to shorter ones, and even to trousers called bloomers.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The craze had one more consequence, which is easy to forget. Cyclists formed clubs which campaigned for better roads, because the surfaces of the time were dreadful. When the first motorists appeared a few years later, they inherited the smooth roads that cyclists had won. Many early car makers had also begun as bicycle makers, and brought their skills with them: steel tubing, ball bearings, chain drives and, of course, tyres filled with air.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: So the bicycle changed far more than the way people travel. That's all for today. Next week, we'll look at how the motor car developed.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.

content: • 1817: built by Karl von Drais, a German {{31}}
• no pedals: the rider pushed along with their feet
• possibly inspired by a shortage of {{32}} for horses
• 1860s: pedals fixed to the front wheel; the rough ride gave it the name '{{34}}'
• high-wheeler: the bigger the wheel, the greater the {{35}} covered with each turn of the pedals
• danger: the rider could be thrown forward, known as taking a '{{36}}'
• 1885: Starley's Rover, with a {{37}} to drive the back wheel
• cyclists' clubs campaigned for better {{40}}, which later helped motorists
